analysis.one_liner: Bans imports of most iron and steel products for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one House member with no cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred, for five years, the entry of nearly all iron and steel articles classified under chapters 72 and 73 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule into the U.S. customs territory. The stated aim, in its title, is to support American steelworkers by cutting off imported steel. It never advanced past its referral to the House Ways and Means Committee's Trade Subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, domestic steel producers and their workers would gain the most, as the import ban would remove foreign competitors from the market for five years. Steelworkers in districts like the sponsor's northern Minnesota could expect stronger job security and pricing power.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits, for five years, the importation of articles classified under chapter 72 or 73 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule — the tariff chapters covering iron, steel, and articles of iron or steel [S3].
The CRS summary states the bill prohibits, for a specified period, importation of certain iron and steel articles [S2].
The bill's short title frames its purpose as supporting steelworkers: the 'Support Our Steelworkers Act of 2015' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industries that buy steel to make products — automakers, appliance makers, construction firms, and manufacturers of pipes, machinery, and equipment — would pay more for steel and face shortages, since the bill covers not just raw steel but finished articles of iron and steel. Households would pay higher prices for cars, appliances, and anything built with steel.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers all articles in tariff chapters 72 and 73, which include finished steel products as well as raw steel, so it would restrict inputs that American manufacturers depend on, not just competing raw material [S3].

A five-year blanket import prohibition, rather than targeted duties or quotas, would raise steel costs for the many more U.S. workers employed in steel-consuming industries than are employed making steel.
Trading partners would likely retaliate or challenge the ban under trade rules, and the bill contains no provisions addressing that exposure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, concentrated gains to steelworkers and steel companies, whose employment and pricing would be protected by removing all foreign competition for five years. But it does so with the bluntest tool available — a total import ban on an entire category of goods — rather than duties or quotas tied to unfair practices. Steel-using manufacturers, which employ far more American workers than steelmaking does, would bear higher input costs and possible shortages, and those costs would reach households through prices. Whether it helps working people overall depends on how you weigh the jobs saved in steel against the jobs and wages put at risk downstream, and the bill itself makes no effort to measure or offset that tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and was never reported out or voted on before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Nolan introduced the bill on November 30, 2015; it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to the Subcommittee on Trade the same day [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: it was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never voted on, and the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, steel-importing firms, steel-using manufacturers, and consumers of steel goods were spared the higher prices and supply constraints the five-year ban would have imposed, while foreign steel producers kept access to the U.S. market. Domestic steelmakers gained nothing, but also lost nothing they already had.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured from the record; the sponsor was a Democrat and the House majority that controlled the committee calendar was Republican.

industries.note: The five-year import ban would remove foreign competition, supporting steel prices, plant utilization, and steelworker jobs. Steelworkers' livelihoods are the group the bill is named for.
These firms buy steel as an input; a blanket ban covering finished articles as well as raw steel would raise their costs and risk supply gaps. Their losses reach consumers through higher prices.
Importers and foreign mills would be shut out of the U.S. market for five years. Their loss is the mechanism by which domestic producers gain.
Households would pay more for cars, appliances, and steel-built goods. Any consumer benefit is indirect and long-run through the health of the domestic steel industry.
